sections.brief: The Arab Revolt from its roots to its suppression, in order: Qassam's death (Nov 1935), the 15 April 1936 killings and the Nablus strike call, the Arab Higher Committee of 25 April 1936 and its cross-factional membership, the six-month strike and its October 1936 end (with the GOC order's own casualty count), the second phase after Lewis Andrews's killing (26 Sept 1937), the outlawing of the committee, the Seychelles deportations and al-Husseini's flight; then British counterinsurgency (20,000 troops, demolitions, 108–122 hangings, collective fines), the Husseini–Nashashibi split and the peace bands (Hughes), and Irgun attacks on Arab civilians (Black Sunday, Ben-Yosef). The death toll is a dispute that must be set out in full: the scene's 2,652 Jews / 618 British / ~5,000 Arabs (attributed to USHMM, not re-verified) against Khalidi's 5,032 Arab dead, the British official figures, and the 400–415 Jewish / 100–200 British figures in Yehudai, JVL and Strickert; log it in SOURCE-CONFLICTS. Present the Palestinian reading (national uprising, brutal repression: Middle East Eye) and the critical reading (rebel violence against Palestinians: Unpacked) side by side, with Hughes's synthesis. Tell the Berlin entity only in a sentence and link forward to rd4_mufti_war; from sq_s04 use only the 1931–1940 entity and keep its 'explains timing, excuses nothing' line. Figures: a timeline of the revolt 1935–39; key figures for the toll with the ranges; embed year_ledger:Part 4:0.

The Peel Commission: appointed August 1936 with six members, report of July 1937; the proposed Jewish state (17% or about 20%, a sourcing difference to state), the Arab state joined to Transjordan, the British zone around Jerusalem. Then the responses side by side: the Twentieth Zionist Congress's deliberate ambiguity (boundaries rejected, principle accepted), the Arab Higher Committee's outright rejection, and Jabotinsky's testimony for both banks of the Jordan (use from gia_src_s02 only the 1925–1930 Revisionist claim and the anthem; link forward for Likud and later). Use sq_s05's 'They rejected every offer' entity to show what the 1937 rejection does and does not prove, and link to the UNSCOP-era comparison. Figure: comparison table of the three responses (Zionist Congress, Arab Higher Committee, Revisionists) and what each accepted or rejected.

Peel's 'exchange of population': the figures as the scene gives them (~225,000 Arabs, ~1,250 Jews, compulsory 'in the last resort', the 1923 Greek–Turkish model), with the research's rounding difference (about 200,000 and 1,000 in Yehudai) noted. The Ben-Gurion letter to Amos (October 1937) must be presented as a disputed reading, with both readings and the fact that historians including Morris changed positions; then what is not disputed (the Twentieth Congress did not reject the clause). Link forward to rd4_labour for the Labour Party's December 1944 'move out' resolution. Figure: key figures of the proposed exchange.

How partition was dropped: the Woodhead Commission (four members, in Palestine April–August 1938), its 9 November 1938 report with Plans A, B and C, Plan C preferred with a customs union, and the British acceptance that partition was politically, administratively and financially impossible. Then the St James's Palace conference of early 1939: the delegations by name, the Arab refusal to sit with the Zionist delegation and the separate meetings, the Maugham committee on the Hussein–McMahon letters, and the failure recorded in the White Paper's own words. Treat the exact opening and closing dates as unverified (they rest on Wikipedia only) and do not print them. Figure: process flow from Peel (1937) to Woodhead (1938) to St James's (1939) to the White Paper.

Évian (6–15 July 1938) country by country, Palestine kept off the agenda at Britain's insistence, Golda Meir as non-participating observer, Trujillo's offer and the 1937 massacre behind it, the Nazi press line 'No one wants them', Weizmann's remark; then Bermuda (April 1943) and the proposal on Palestine not considered. Close on the argument the closed doors gave the movement, and on Britain holding the one door. Figure: comparison table of what each country said at Évian.

Wingate's Special Night Squads (Ein Harod, June–October 1938; about 75 Haganah volunteers including Dayan, Allon and Kopel), the night-raid doctrine and Uri Avnery's critique (attributed), the same administration jailing Dayan in 1939; then the Palmach (May 1941, British cooperation that receded after El Alamein), the Jewish Brigade Group (1944; Italy, March 1945) and the Haganah's 1947 strength. The Brigade and wartime volunteering are thin in the research: tell only what the scene holds and say plainly that numbers of volunteers are not given here. Embed global_funding:Defense Money:0 and discuss its 1938 Kofer HaYishuv levy and the 1939 £80,000 defense line in a £720,000 Jewish Agency budget (cite the dashboard's source scene gf_s02 by link, not by drawing it). Figure: timeline 1938–1947 of British–Haganah cooperation and arrests.

Aliyah Bet from the founding of Mossad LeAliyah Bet in 1938 and the separate Revisionist voyages, through the wartime voyages, to the postwar Brihah, Cyprus internment (about 52,000 by 1948; last camp closed February 1949) and Exodus 1947. Tell the pre-1945 part fully and the postwar part as an epilogue that links forward. Present both truths the scene names: desperate survivors and an organized state-in-waiting. Embed prestate_funding:People:1 and money_1948:Land & People:2 and discuss 376,415 recorded Jewish immigrants 1920–1946 against the scene's ~480,000 total Mandate-era immigration (legal and illegal) and well over 100,000 clandestine. Figure: key figures (142 voyages, over 90% intercepted, ~52,000 interned, 70,000+ survivors).

The practical questions as of 1938: who the American leaders were (citizens acting legally), Ben-Gurion's New York years 1915–18, Golda Meir's Milwaukee, ocean liners and the first transatlantic flying boats (1939), and the Foreign Agents Registration Act of 1938. Keep it short; link forward to fa_s01 for enforcement and to the 1962 order.

Kristallnacht, 9–10 November 1938: Grynszpan and the Zbąszyń deportations, vom Rath's death, Goebbels and state coordination across Germany, Austria and the Sudetenland, the 1,400+ synagogues and 7,500 businesses, 30,000 men to the camps (Wachsmann's phrase), at least 91 murdered with a true toll in the hundreds, the collective fine, and Roosevelt's recall of his ambassador on 15 November. Tie it to Évian four months earlier and to the White Paper six months later. Figure: key figures; timeline 7–15 November 1938.

What the Vatican's authority covered and did not (the magisterium, imprimatur, the Reformation split), stated as background to the wartime question in the next section. Keep it short; this is the frame, not a finding.

Pius XII from his election in March 1939 through the war: the undisputed absence of a public condemnation naming Jews or Nazism, the exact language of the 1942 Christmas address, the documented sheltering in Rome, and the historians' competing explanations, each in its strongest form, with no verdict. From vat_s00d use only the 1929 Lateran settlement (the $92.1 million, Francesco Pacelli as negotiator, Nogara) and its explicit limit: financial context is not proof of motive. Figure: comparison table of the two documented sides of the record.

The White Paper of 17 May 1939 from its own text: no Jewish state, an independent Palestine state within ten years, 75,000 immigrants over five years (10,000 a year plus 25,000 refugees), Arab acquiescence after five years, land-transfer powers, and the one-third population ceiling. Then its reception, each side in its own terms: Amery, Churchill ('an act of repudiation') and Morrison in the Commons; Weizmann's 31 May letter and the Jewish Agency's legal case; the US consul general's report of Arab relief and Jewish bitterness; the Arab Higher Committee's rejection. Then the Permanent Mandates Commission (8–29 June 1939; unanimous on interpretation, four to three on conformity), the war intervening before the League Council could act, the July 1939 quota suspension, and Ben-Gurion's 'as if there were no White Paper' line (attributed). Use s07b's White Paper entity and its deep dive here. Do not print the Commons division figures (unverified). Embed prestate_funding:People:0 and discuss the Jewish share of 17% (1931) and 33% (1946) against the one-third ceiling. Figures: comparison of the Mandate's Article 6 and the White Paper's immigration terms; timeline May–September 1939.

Roosevelt's wartime position as the record shows it: Wise 'surprised and shocked', the approved State Department plan to suppress public discussion of Palestine for the war's duration, the October 1945 State Department release calling the Ibn Saud letter one of 'several letters' to Arab leaders, and the two registers (public warmth, private caution). Make the case for each reading of FDR. Link forward to s07ca for the Quincy meeting itself. Figure: comparison of public messages and private commitments.

The ships the White Paper turned away: the Patria (Haifa, November 1940; 267–268 killed by a Haganah bomb meant to disable the engines; how it is remembered), the Struma (24 February 1942; over 780 dead, one survivor; likely a Soviet submarine), and Exodus 1947 as a short epilogue linked forward to ab_s01 and the UNSCOP period. Present the Exodus-and-the-vote dispute both ways as the scene does. Figure: timeline of the three ships; key figures.

Lehi's split from the Irgun, the Ankara document of 11 January 1941 (the offer, the courier, von Hentig, no German reply), Lord Moyne's killing in Cairo on 6 November 1944, the hangings of March 1945, Churchill's 'no message', the mainstream denunciation as 'traitors', and the later reburial on Mount Herzl under Shamir. Link to the rd3 account of the Irgun and Lehi (s07e2) and to the 1944–45 'Hunting Season' there rather than retelling it. Figure: timeline 1940–1945.

Al-Husseini's war, told as one man's documented choices: exile from 1937, Iraq, the Rashid Ali coup and its collapse, the Farhud of 1–2 June 1941 (USHMM's 150–180 killed, 600 injured, ~1,500 homes and stores looted, with the higher estimates noted as such; Volume I's account in s00e2 gives at least 128 and up to 180 killed and over 1,000 injured: link to it with [scene:s00e2|…] and say the counts differ), then Berlin from 1941, the meeting with Hitler, propaganda and Waffen-SS recruitment, and his fate after the war (from s07a5's Berlin entity and its deep dive). Add from the research that Jamal al-Husseini joined the 1941 Iraqi revolt and was interned, and that Husseini-backed gunmen killed Fakhri Nashashibi in Iraq in 1941. Keep the scene's explicit discipline: not a statement about Palestinians as a people. The finer record (date of the Hitler meeting, the SS division's name, letters opposing the emigration of Jewish children, the dispute over his role in the Holocaust) is not yet researched: do not add it; state that the section covers the documented core only.

Hillel Kook as 'Peter Bergson' from 1940: the Committee for a Jewish Army (1941), the Emergency Committee (1943), the Hebrew Committee of National Liberation; the full-page advertisements; 'We Will Never Die' (9 March 1943, about 40,000 people); the rabbis' march (6 October 1943); the Treasury report and the War Refugee Board (Executive Order 9417, January 1944; estimates of lives saved vary); the opposition of Wise and the mainstream; the pivot to statehood and the Irgun. From bwm_s01 use only Benzion Netanyahu's arrival in 1940 and his years running the Revisionists' American operation; link forward for the rest. Embed the info_war map and discuss its two machines. Figure: timeline 1940–1944.

Who Washington watched in the war years: FARA (1938), the Bergson group's June 1944 registration as agent of the 'Hebrew nation', the deportation proceedings, the State Department–instigated FBI investigation (informants, mail, trash; the Wyman Institute's FOIA files), mainstream leaders urging his deportation; and the OSS Foreign Nationalities Branch's Palestine desk (from fis_s04 and cia_s01: tell only the wartime OSS and the 1940 founding of the Shai; present cia_s01's claims of 'deliberate tolerance' and Rekhesh non-prosecution as that scene's interpretation, attributed, and note Rekhesh's main activity falls after 1945). From df_s08 use only the 1938 law and the contrast it draws; link forward for NORAID and AIPAC. Tell the 1949 convictions and the pardons briefly and link forward. Figure: comparison table of who was watched and who was not, 1938–1945.

Wannsee from its own Protocol: Göring's order of 31 July 1941, the 20 January 1942 meeting (fifteen officials, about ninety minutes, Heydrich chairing, the 11 million figure), no recorded objection, Eichmann's editing, and the Protocol's later use at Nuremberg and in Jerusalem. State precisely what the meeting was and was not. Figure: process flow from the July 1941 order to implementation.

Biltmore, 6–11 May 1942: why it was held in New York (no Congress possible), who was in the room (about 600 delegates from 18 countries), the language change from 'national home' to 'Jewish Commonwealth' and Medoff's reading of the word, the Weizmann–Ben-Gurion contest, and the October 1942 ratification by the Zionist General Council (from s07c) that made it binding until late 1946. The White Paper entity is told in rd4_white_paper; refer to it in a clause. Jewish dissent from Biltmore (the American Council for Judaism, Ihud, the American Jewish Conference of 1943) is not researched here: say so and link to s00b3 for the binationalist critique. Figure: comparison of Balfour 1917, the White Paper 1939 and Biltmore 1942.

How six million is known: Hilberg's 5.1 million and Dawidowicz's 5,933,900 as independent methods, Yad Vashem's ~4.8 million named victims, Auschwitz (1.3 million deported, 1.1 million murdered), liberation on 27 January 1945, and USHMM's account of denial. Close the five-part arc as the scene does. The Yishuv's response to the news (from November 1942) is not yet researched: state this as a gap rather than fill it. Figure: key figures; comparison of the estimation methods.

The American Zionist Emergency Council from August 1943: Silver and Wise as co-chairs, Silver's break from quiet diplomacy, then the method from AZEC's own files (azc_s02): local Emergency Committees directed from 342 Madison Avenue, sample letters timed to 'pour into Washington', the telegram campaigns on Sol Bloom, America and Palestine sent to every member of Congress (nearly 400 members of the 78th Congress), and the critic's report about Wagner's mail (attributed). Present the 'organized, not spontaneous' finding alongside the scene's point that the sympathy was real. Embed the info_war and state_build maps; embed global_funding:Year by Year:1 and global_funding:Overview:0 and discuss the United Jewish Appeal's wartime giving ($124M+ in 1939–45). Figure: process flow of a letter campaign; link forward for 1945–48.

Palestine in Congress and the parties, 1944–45, one story: the Wright–Compton and Wagner–Taft resolutions, the House hearings with Rabbi Lazaron's opposition, Marshall and Stimson's request to defer (March 1944), the platforms ('the first time in American history'), Stimson's letter to Taft days before the election, House committee approval on 30 November, deferral again at the State Department's insistence, and the December 1945 concurrent resolution with its 'equal rights' wording. Use cg_s01's 1918–1948 frame briefly (Lodge–Fish backward link; no vote to create or recognize). Figure: timeline January 1944–December 1945; comparison of the 1944 text and the 1945 text.

Roosevelt's health and the 1944 election: Bruenn's diagnosis of 28 March 1944, McIntire's public assurances, the Lahey memo of 10 July 1944 and its sixty years in a vault, Truman kept in the dark, and why the vice-presidential choice mattered; the 'Missouri Compromise' reasons for Truman with the explicit note that no evidence ties the choice to his finances. Figure: timeline March 1944–April 1945.

Henry Wallace and Zionism: his 1930s conviction through Lowdermilk, the documented reasons for his removal in July 1944 (ideology, not Palestine; the 65% Gallup figure), and, briefly, his 1948 campaign against Truman's embargo and the New York Jewish vote, linked forward. Set the common assumption against the record. Figure: comparison of the assumed and documented story.

The Great Bitter Lake meeting of 14 February 1945 aboard the USS Quincy: why it happened (the existing oil relationship), the roughly five-hour meeting, Ibn Saud's objection (Jews to be given land in Germany), FDR's assurance and his letter of 5 April 1945, and the later departure from it under Truman, told without speculation about what FDR would have done. From isa_src_s01 add the memorandum's drafting by Eddy and Yassin, its publication in FRUS, and Ibn Saud's follow-up letter. Figure: timeline February–April 1945.

The British side as the war ended: the Labour Party's record against the 1939 White Paper (Attlee, Dalton, Morrison), its December 1944 conference resolution (majority immigration, 'Let the Arabs be encouraged to move out, as the Jews move in', boundary extension), Labour's victory in July 1945, and the State Department's 30 July 1945 forecast that Labour would modify the White Paper but not implement the resolution. Tie back to pl_s01 (transfer on paper in 1937) and forward to Stage Five. Bevin's appointment and the wartime Colonial Secretaries and High Commissioners are not yet researched: do not name them beyond what the sources here hold. Figure: comparison of the 1944 resolution and the July 1945 forecast.
